about.notAdvice: Stoafi is a planning aid and general education, not financial advice. Decisions about your money are yours.

gold.what: A metal people have trusted for thousands of years; it pays no interest and its price swings.
gold.risk: The price moves with the world, the dollar and fear; it can stay flat for years.
gold.cost: The gap between buying and selling price, plus craftsmanship cost for jewellery.
gold.horizon: Long term, as a small part of what you own.
gold.mistake: Putting most of your money in one thing because it has been rising.

currency.what: Money of another country, kept as cash or in an account.
currency.risk: Its value against your own currency changes daily; it earns no interest at home.
currency.cost: The gap between the bank's buying and selling rate.
currency.horizon: Short to medium term, or to cover costs paid in that currency.
currency.mistake: Buying after a big jump and selling in a panic when it dips.

stock.what: A small piece of ownership in one company.
stock.risk: One company can lose most of its value; prices swing a lot, day to day and year to year.
stock.cost: Broker commission and, in some countries, tax on gains.
stock.horizon: Five years or more, and only money you will not need soon.
stock.mistake: Betting on one or two companies instead of spreading out.

fund.what: A pool of money that a manager invests in many things for you.
fund.risk: Depends on what it holds; a fund of shares is far riskier than one of bonds.
fund.cost: A yearly management fee that comes out of your return whether the fund does well or not.
fund.horizon: Match it to what the fund holds: shares need years, bonds need less.
fund.mistake: Choosing by last year's return and ignoring the fee.

index-fund.what: A fund that simply copies a market index, such as the largest companies, instead of picking winners.
index-fund.risk: It falls when the market falls, but you are spread across hundreds of companies.
index-fund.cost: Usually the lowest fees of any fund, which matters a great deal over decades.
index-fund.horizon: Ten years or more, bought steadily month after month.
index-fund.mistake: Selling when the market drops, which locks in the loss.

bond.what: A loan you give to a government or company that pays you interest and returns the money on a set date.
bond.risk: The issuer might fail to pay, and prices fall when interest rates rise.
bond.cost: Usually small commissions; check the tax on the interest.
bond.horizon: Until the maturity date, or as the steady part of a mix.
bond.mistake: Chasing the highest interest without asking why it is so high.

deposit.what: Money kept in a bank for a fixed time at a promised rate.
deposit.risk: Very low risk to your money, but inflation can still eat the real value.
deposit.cost: Usually free, but breaking it early can cost you the interest.
deposit.horizon: Short term, and for money you need in a known month.
deposit.mistake: Leaving a lot there for years while prices rise faster than interest.

crypto.what: Digital coins that live on networks rather than being issued by a bank or government.
crypto.risk: Prices can fall by half within months, and exchanges or wallets can be hacked or fail.
crypto.cost: Exchange fees and the spread; tax rules differ and often change.
crypto.horizon: Only an amount you could lose without it changing your life.
crypto.mistake: Borrowing to buy, or following a hyped coin.

real-estate.what: A home, shop or land you own, for living in or renting out.
real-estate.risk: Hard to sell quickly, and one property is a big bet on one place.
real-estate.cost: Taxes, notary and agent fees, repairs and time spent managing it.
real-estate.horizon: Many years; it is hard to get out of quickly.
real-estate.mistake: Counting the rent but forgetting repairs, empty months and taxes.

other.what: Anything else you own for its value, such as art, wine or a business share.
other.risk: Often hard to value and hard to sell, so the price you see may not be a price you can get.
other.cost: Varies a lot; ask what it costs to sell.
other.horizon: Think about how you would turn it back into cash.
other.mistake: Trusting a number you cannot actually sell at.
